paper_metadata.title: Hot Compression Behavior and Tensile Property of a Novel Ni–Co-Based Superalloy Prepared by Electron Beam Smelting Layered Solidification Technology

evidence.quote: The hot compression behavior and tensile strength after compression of a new Ni–Co-based superalloy produced using elec- tron beam smelting layered (EBSL) solidification technology were investigated.

The initial microstructures of the homogenized heat-treated EBSL-alloy, as seen in Fig. 2a–c, consists mainly of coarse γ grain and some large size annealing twins (Fig. 2a).

When soaking at 1120 °C, partial γ′ phases were redissolved into the matrix and the residual γ′ phases exhibited a sub-spherical or sub-square shape with an average the size of approximately 430 nm.

The results show a higher DRX degree at strain rate of 0.01 s−1 compared to that at 1 s−1, indicating a higher fraction of DRX grains at lower strain rates. At high strain rate, DRX grains mainly distribute along GBs discontinuously.

At a high temperature, the slip systems in the alloy become more readily activated, make it more likely for dislocations to move toward GBs, resulting in increased formation of HAGB (black lines in Fig. 5e–h).
A high density of LAGB (gray lines in Fig. 5g, h) is observed, particularly near the original GBs.

The results revealed that this EBSL technology accelerates dynamic recrystallization (DRX), without compromising the strength of alloy.
This suggests that DDRX is the dominate DRX mechanism under conditions of low strain rate.

At γ′ super-solvus temperature, the orientation gradients along GBs and across the grain interior are reversed. This indicates that CDRX occurred frequently, as supported by the presence of individual or clustered grains within the original grain.

evidence.quote: Secondly, fine DRX grains at a lower deformation temperature are a result of the pinning effect on GBs caused by the undissolved γ′ particles.
During the initial stage of deformation, the flow stress increased rapidly due to work hardening, driven by a rapid rise in dislocation density.
As deformation progressed, flow stresses increased more gradually until reaching maximal values, at which point dynamic softening mechanisms counteracted work hardening behavior.
